payload.claim: Across a sample of 1,150 World Cup games, a country's elimination from the World Cup is associated with an average 0.5% decline in that country's stock market, controlling for prior-day momentum and other factors.
payload.quote:
So I looked at 1,150 games. What I found was a systematic pattern.
When a country gets eliminated from the World Cup, then the market goes down by, on average, half a percent, even when you control for the energy field or momentum, which is what the market did on the last day, and many other factors.

source.title: Can a World Cup Loss Move the Stock Market?

data_required: World Cup match results and elimination dates by country, 1,150-game sample
national stock market index daily returns around elimination dates
testability.notes: Original academic paper (referenced but not the source document itself) presumably contains full methodology; this quote gives the core testable proposition.

payload.claim: When England was eliminated from the World Cup by Argentina, the English stock market opened lower the following Monday despite positive economic news, with financial media attributing the decline partly to the World Cup defeat.
payload.quote: So interesting, when England was knocked out by Argentina, the market on the open on the Monday, even though there was positive economic news. And if you look at Yahoo Finance, which is a respectable source of news, they were attributing it, in part, due to the World Cup defeat.

source.title: Can a World Cup Loss Move the Stock Market?

data_required: date of England's World Cup elimination by Argentina
UK stock market index (e.g., FTSE) opening/return data for the following Monday
concurrent UK economic news releases for that period
testability.notes: Specific single-event example supporting the broader systematic claim.

payload.claim: In the case of Brazil's 7-1 loss to Germany in the World Cup, the Brazilian stock market rose rather than fell, contrary to the typical elimination-day decline pattern, attributed to political reasoning that the president's (left-wing) political standing would be damaged by the loss, which markets viewed as favorable.
payload.quote:
With one big exception, which is when Brazil lost 7-1 to Germany. So even though this was 12 years ago, it may still be such a shocking result. Actually, the market went up.
Why? For a different reason. The president of Brazil, Dilma Rousseff, she had her identity linked to the team.
She’d built a lot of stadiums, which were earmarked for schools and hospitals. And so the view was that if Brazil got knocked out really badly, she might not last another presidency. And because she was seen as left-wing, then that was seen as good for the economy.

source.title: Can a World Cup Loss Move the Stock Market?

data_required: date of Brazil's 7-1 loss to Germany
Brazilian stock market index (e.g., Bovespa) return around that date
contemporaneous news/political commentary linking the result to the president
testability.notes: This is a counter-example/exception to the general World Cup elimination effect claim, driven by fundamentals rather than sentiment.

payload.claim: In a simple analytically solvable model of trend following strategy, the trend follower loses more often than it gains, and this produces a specific analytical shape for the distribution of profit per trade.
payload.quote:
on Trend Followers Lose More Often Than They Gain: Wilmott Magazine Article – Marc Potters & Jean-Philippe Bouchaud
We solve exactly a simple model of trend following strategy, and obtain the analytical shape of the profit per trade distribution.

source.title: https://www.wilmott.com/trend-followers-lose-more-often-than-they-gain-wilmott-magazine-article-marc-potters-jean-philippe-bouchaud/

data_required: trade-level P&L records for a trend-following strategy
historical price series for the underlying market(s) used to generate trend signals
testability.notes: Document is largely a webpage index; only the article abstract carries a testable proposition, and it references a theoretical model without specifying asset class, horizon, or parameters, so backtest specifics must be inferred.

payload.claim: A probit model using the 10yr-3mo term spread and short rate, estimated on 1960-2018 data, with a 33% recession-probability threshold, correctly signals every NBER-defined US recession from 1960 to 2018 (excluding the pandemic recession) but produces a false positive for 2024.
payload.quote: Using a 33% threshold and the pre-2018 sample, the term spread catches every post-1960 recession (taking the pandemic recession was not a typical recession), but gives the false positive for 2024.

source.title: The Term Spread As Recession Predictor, Post-2024

payload.claim: A probit model using the 10yr-3mo term spread and short rate, estimated over the full sample through 2026M08 (assuming no recession occurs by that date), fails to signal the 1990-91, 2001, and 2007-09 recessions at the 33% threshold and still produces a false positive for 2024.
payload.quote: The full sample regression (assumes no recession appears by 2026M08) no longer catches the 1990-91, 2001, and 2007-09 recessions, and still provides a false positive for 2024.

source.title: The Term Spread As Recession Predictor, Post-2024

payload.claim: Extending the probit model's estimation sample to the full period (versus the 1960-2018 sample) reduces its pseudo-R2 from 0.30 to 0.25.
payload.quote: In other respects, the full sample regression is less successful; the pseudo-R2 drops from 0.30 to 0.25.

source.title: The Term Spread As Recession Predictor, Post-2024

payload.text:
correction-2026-09-30-pbo-family-kill: Five strategies were buried by the PBO family kill under verdicts labelled gauntlet-protocol-v6, although v6 states that the family kill is retired. The implementation did not match the chained protocol. This note records what the chain says, what the code did, what was measured when the five were re-judged on their own gates, and what happens to them. It changes no verdict and no state on the chain. The chain is append-only, and the five graveyard entries stand.

WHAT THE CHAIN SAYS. The gauntlet-protocol-v6 note, registry entry 2514 (2026-08-20T22:36:42Z), states: "pbo and pbo_underpowered leave FAIL_ORDER, and the family kill is retired." Its battery is six gates, each a property of the individual strategy alone: sharpe_floor, oos_negative, edge_decay, mc_p05, p_ruin and cost_stress. The same note declares that every individual edge must be standalone when running through the gauntlet, and that a configuration is judged on its own evidence.

WHAT THE CODE DID. Every commit time in this note is UTC, as the chain's times are. The family kill entered gauntlet.py under protocol-v4 as killed_groups (commit 52829359, 2026-08-17T21:21Z), and protocol-v5 rebuilt its trigger as PBO_KILL_PCTILE at 0.95 (commit eeec3f66, 2026-08-20T08:21Z). The v6 build (commit 30e30652, 2026-08-20T23:00Z) took pbo and pbo_underpowered out of FAIL_ORDER and left the family kill untouched. After the six gates had run, a family whose observed PBO sat at or above the 0.95 percentile of its own permutation null was marked killed, and every member of it that had passed all six gates was failed with the reason pbo_family_kill. The kill could not bury a strategy that had failed a gate of its own, so it fired only on strategies that had passed all six. The flag pbo_family_kill was written to every member of a killed family, which is why 91 v6 verdicts carry it at the time of this note; 86 of those 91 failed a gate of their own first (84 on sharpe_floor and 2 on oos_negative) and were buried for that gate. Five were buried for pbo_family_kill.

THE FIVE. Each verdict is a gauntlet verdict labelled gauntlet-protocol-v6 with verdict fail and pbo_family_kill true; each burial is a state_change from gauntlet to graveyard with the reason pbo_family_kill. Times are the chain's ts_utc.
b09adeb0be6faf4e: verdict at entry 10367 (2026-08-25T23:25:39Z), buried at entry 11017 (2026-08-25T23:27:51Z).
9acf68e5a2ef607d: verdict at entry 10378 (2026-08-25T23:25:41Z), buried at entry 11028 (2026-08-25T23:27:54Z).
7ecf180b7e8b05ce: verdict at entry 10388 (2026-08-25T23:25:43Z), buried at entry 11038 (2026-08-25T23:27:56Z).
6aebc4b7f051baba: verdict at entry 10396 (2026-08-25T23:25:45Z), buried at entry 11046 (2026-08-25T23:27:57Z).
15595642e7a2caaa: verdict at entry 31008 (2026-09-03T21:23:03Z), buried at entry 32011 (2026-09-03T21:32:23Z).

WHAT WAS MEASURED. Each of the five was re-judged by the standalone six-gate battery that the v6.1 worker uses, on price bars truncated at the data_end recorded in its verdict's artifact bundle (config.json, committed by the verdict's artifacts_hash), with the gauntlet's own simulation and the same cutoff. All five PASS. Their chained basis is fail with the burial reason pbo_family_kill, so all five cleared every gate of their own and were buried by the family kill alone. The same comparison was run on a random sample of 60 verdicts that the family kill did not touch (seed 20260930, drawn from the 3,272 such v6 verdicts on the chain at the time of this note) together with the five. All 65 verdicts are identical to the chained ones: for the five, a pass against a base pass buried by the family kill, and for the sample, the same pass or the same failing gate.

THE PARITY RULE, AS ACCEPTED: identical verdicts, and metrics bit-identical when compared under the same engine revision. WHAT WAS COMPARED: the parity tool (tools/gauntlet_parity.py) compares exactly eleven per-strategy gate metrics: is_edge_per_trade, oos_edge_per_trade, edge_decay_pct, mc_p05_equity, p_ruin, cost_stress_net_pnl, train_sharpe, is_edge_raw, oos_edge_raw, is_vol and oos_vol. On those eleven, 54 of the 65 are bit-identical. The other 11 differ in train_sharpe, and in some of them in other metrics computed from the same return series, by at most 17 units in the last place. The largest differences by metric are train_sharpe 17 units in the last place, oos_edge_per_trade and oos_edge_raw 5, edge_decay_pct 3, is_edge_per_trade and is_edge_raw 2, and mc_p05_equity 1. WHAT WAS NOT COMPARED: the tool does not compare the other recorded metrics, including the purged walk-forward report, the era summary, the regime split, the perturbation and, where a verdict carries them, the exit-reason counts (exit_reasons_is, exit_reasons_oos), open_at_end and the benchmark_relative block, so the claim of bit-identity above does not extend to them. A separate recomputation of the 65 covered every per-strategy metric that both the chained verdict and the standalone battery carry, except the perturbation, which it did not recompute. It found a difference in those other metrics only in the 11 above and in one verdict that matched on all eleven gate metrics, a5ceb9a0050a0ad8, whose walk-forward fold 1 net differs by one unit in the last place (0.5228214664922483 chained, 0.5228214664922481 recomputed). WHERE THE DIFFERENCE COMES FROM: all 11 are verdicts dated 2026-08-24 or 2026-08-25. Commit 74b9703b (2026-08-26T23:19Z) changed the engine's arithmetic, replacing statistics.stdev at its two call sites with a float two-pass sample standard deviation, and ENGINE_REV "e2" was introduced with it; the engine before it carried no revision constant. At the time of this note 818 v6 gauntlet verdicts on the chain are dated before that commit. 17 of them are among the 65 compared, and of those 17, 11 differ on the eleven gate metrics and 6 are bit-identical on them. All 48 compared verdicts dated after the commit are bit-identical on the eleven. Run on the same bars with the engine as it stood before 74b9703b, all 11 reproduce every per-strategy metric that both the chained verdict and the standalone battery carry bit for bit, except the perturbation, which that run did not recompute, and the protocol label. One of the five, b09adeb0be6faf4e, is among the 11: its chained train_sharpe is 0.5434340322749764 and the standalone value is 0.5434340322749766, one unit in the last place apart, and its verdict is unchanged. None of the differences changes a verdict.

WHAT HAPPENS TO THE FIVE. Their graveyard entries stand. Nothing is moved out of the graveyard, and nothing re-opens a closed verdict, for the reason v6 gives: re-judging closed verdicts under a later standard is the failure mode this chain exists to prevent. Each of the five is instead re-tried as a NEW strategy id through the existing D9 re-trial path, once the standalone gauntlet worker is live. A re-trial is a new registration, charged to N in full, and it is judged by all six gates from scratch on the data then current. It inherits nothing from the buried entry, neither its verdict nor its passing of the gates. The burial and the re-trial both stay on the chain, so a later reader can see the five were buried for a reason v6 had retired and were then tried again as new strategies.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM. It does not claim the five have edge. Passing six standalone gates is what the protocol asks of a strategy before quarantine, and v6 states that a looser gauntlet producing survivors is not evidence of edge. Only the forward record in quarantine can say, and only after it exists. No other strategy was affected by the mismatch: at the time of this note the other 86 family-flagged verdicts failed a gate of their own and were buried for it, and the 3,272 unflagged v6 verdicts (also at the time of this note) were never in a killed family. The statement that verdicts under v6 were standalone was false for these five, and this note is the correction of that statement on the chain.

WHAT CHANGES FROM HERE. The gauntlet-protocol-v6.1 note, chained with this one, records that the family kill is not applied from that note onward and that verify_registry.py rejects it at any later chain line. The five burials before that note remain valid chain history.

gauntlet-protocol-v6.1: Supersedes gauntlet-protocol-v6 only in WHEN the registry-wide recorded statistics are written. Everything else in v6, chained at registry entry 2514, stands as written. Every verdict judged before this note stands, and so does every state change those verdicts produced. This is an addendum, not a new battery: no gate is added, removed or re-tuned, and no threshold moves. Pre-declared before the first verdict labelled v6.1 exists. The gauntlet worker refuses to write a verdict until this note is on the chain.

THE CHANGE, AND ONLY THE CHANGE. Under v6 every gauntlet verdict was written together with registry-wide statistics: the effective-trials count trials_n, the count of registered strategies registered_n, the deflated Sharpe, the observed PBO with its null percentile, plateau_ok and the Harvey-Liu haircut. Computing them means re-simulating and clustering every registered strategy. Under v6 not one of them gated, and v6.1 keeps it that way: no gate reads any of them. A verdict labelled v6.1 is written when the candidate's own six gates have run, carries metrics.protocol equal to gauntlet-protocol-v6.1, and does not wait for any of those statistics.

WHAT A v6.1 VERDICT CARRIES. Every per-strategy metric v6 recorded that is a property of the strategy alone: the in-sample and out-of-sample edge per trade and the raw edges, the volatilities, the edge decay, mc_p05_equity, p_ruin, cost_stress_net_pnl, train_sharpe, the era summary, the exit reasons, the purged walk-forward report and the regime split, the last two each still carrying their window key, and the other fields that describe the strategy alone. It does not carry deflated_sharpe, trials_n, registered_n, expected_max_sharpe, the trials alignment fields, any PBO field, pbo_family_kill, plateau_ok, haircut or sibling_group_n. sibling_group_n, the one group-level count v6 kept as provenance, is therefore no longer written to the verdict, and it is not part of the statistics entry either. The artifact bundle keeps the cutoff and the per-cell data_end exactly as before.

WHERE THE STATISTICS GO. A later chain entry of type gauntlet_stats records them, one per v6.1 gauntlet verdict, linked to that verdict by verdict_entry_hash. It carries trials_n, trials_n_raw, trials_n_floor, trials_n_floor_entry_hash, registered_n, deflated_sharpe, pbo, pbo_percentile, plateau_ok, haircut, cluster_method, data_vintage, data_digest and data_end_by_cell, together with the quantities the deflated Sharpe was computed from. It records and never changes a strategy's state. It is written by a separate job, and it may follow its verdict by days. No gate, state change or promotion waits on it. verify_registry.py rejects a gauntlet_stats entry that does not point at an earlier v6.1 gauntlet verdict of the same strategy, and a second entry for one verdict.

WHAT A RECORDED STATISTIC DESCRIBES. A gauntlet_stats entry describes the registry and the price data as they stood at its own data_vintage, not as they stood on the day of the verdict. data_vintage is a date, the most recent Sunday on or before the run, and the job reads each price file truncated at that date. data_digest is computed by data_digest_of in pipeline/gauntlet_stats.py, over every cell the run read, which is every cell of every registered strategy. For each cell, bars_through_sha256 takes the hex sha256 of that cell's price file cut at data_vintage: the header line, then every row whose first field, compared by its first ten characters, is on or before data_vintage, in file order, with line endings normalised to LF and every line ending in LF. data_digest is then the hex sha256 of the UTF-8 text made of one line per cell, sorted by cell id, each line being the cell id (asset, underscore, timeframe), a colon and that cell's hash, and each ending in LF. data_end_by_cell gives the last bar of each of the strategy's own cells. The vintage names a Sunday but does not pin the bars, because rows dated on or before that Sunday can still arrive during the week for some series, fx and equity ETF data among them. Two entries on one vintage can therefore rest on different data, and the digest is what tells them apart. registered_n counts every registered strategy at the run. The deflated Sharpe is computed over the return series v6 used, and cluster_method names the clustering method.

HOW trials_n IS RECORDED. The clustering method is unchanged from protocol-v3: k is the cluster count that maximises the silhouette quality score, the mean of the silhouette values divided by their standard deviation, over k from 2 to n minus 1, for the correlation-distance clustering of the daily-return series of every registered strategy, every buried one included. That argmax is recorded as trials_n_raw. The effective trials used for the recorded deflated Sharpe and for the Harvey-Liu haircut is trials_n, the larger of trials_n_raw and trials_n_floor. trials_n_floor is the highest cluster count already on this chain: trials_n on gauntlet verdicts under protocols v3, v4, v5 and v6, and trials_n_raw on earlier gauntlet_stats entries. Registration counts recorded under v2 are excluded. The entry that supplied the floor is named by trials_n_floor_entry_hash. From this note onward, trials_n never falls from one gauntlet_stats entry to a later one. THE REASON IS A MEASURED FACT. On a registry that only grew, the argmax moved from 302 at 6,075 registered strategies to 480 at 11,476 and then to 44 at 11,835, and a falling N would make the recorded deflated Sharpe more lenient as more strategies had been tried. The 302 at 6,075 is chained. The 480 at 11,476 and the 44 at 11,835 come from the loop's run logs, and the 2026-09-28 run that logged the 480 chained no verdict. At the time of this note the highest value on the chain is 302, recorded by 1,003 v6 gauntlet verdicts, the first of them at registry entry 30782 (2026-09-03T21:21:06Z). trials_sr_var is computed from the current clustering and is not floored. Nothing here changes a gate: the deflated Sharpe and the haircut are recorded and do not gate.

THE VERDICTS THAT ALREADY RECORDED N = 44. At the time of this note, 676 gauntlet-protocol-v6 verdicts at registry entries 66700 to 67375 (2026-09-30T22:11Z to 2026-09-30T22:22Z, registered_n 11,860; 672 fail and 4 pass) recorded trials_n 44, so the deflated Sharpe and the haircut recorded on them used N = 44, after 1,003 verdicts that recorded 302. Those verdicts stand, as every verdict judged before this note stands. No gate depended on N for any of them. The floor applies to gauntlet_stats entries from this note onward and does not rewrite them.

THE FAMILY KILL IS NOT APPLIED. v6 states that the family kill is retired. The v6 implementation did not retire it, and five strategies were buried by it under verdicts labelled v6. That failure and its handling are recorded in the correction note chained with this one. From this note onward no gauntlet verdict applies the family kill, and verify_registry.py rejects any gauntlet verdict that carries pbo_family_kill true, and any state change that gives pbo_family_kill as its reason, at any chain line after this note. The five v6 burials before it stay valid chain history, and the verifier does not reach them.

GATES RETAINED, UNCHANGED, IN THIS ORDER: sharpe_floor at 0.4 on the train window, oos_negative, edge_decay above minus 25 percent on volatility-normalized per-trade edge, mc_p05 above 1.0, p_ruin below 0.05, cost_stress positive at double slippage. Six gates, each a property of the individual strategy and computable without reference to any sibling, any group or any registry-wide statistic. The screen is untouched: screen-protocol-v1 keeps its 2023-12-31 train fence, its floor of 40 trades and its requirement of net above zero after costs.

RATCHET POSITION. Against v6 as chained, this note changes nothing a gate decides, so it neither loosens nor tightens the battery. It changes when recorded numbers are written and which numbers a verdict itself carries. Against what the v6 implementation actually did, applying the six gates alone is a loosening for the five strategies the family kill buried, and the correction note says what happens to them. No threshold is tightened anywhere to compensate. The multiplicity warning in v6 is unchanged: more survivors than v5 produced would be evidence of a looser gate and not of edge, and the deflated Sharpe at 0.95 on the forward record remains the place where the search burden is priced.

payload.claim: U.S. supplier stocks experience a cumulative abnormal return of approximately -3.6 percent in the days following the announcement that one or more of their Chinese customers are added to a U.S. export-control list, with most of the decline occurring within the first five trading days.
payload.quote: The chart below shows that, in our data, U.S. suppliers experience a cumulative abnormal stock return of −3.6 percent right after the announcement that export controls target one or more of their Chinese customers, with most of the decline occurring during the first five trading days.

source.locator: section: Export Controls as Geoeconomic Shocks
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

testability.notes: Based on Fama-French five-factor model abnormal returns per chart notes.

payload.claim: Among mutual funds, conditional on an export control event, a one standard deviation increase (2.5 percentage points) in a fund's exposure to affected U.S. suppliers is associated with a 22-basis-point decline in monthly fund returns.
payload.quote: Conditional on an export control event, a one standard deviation increase in exposure (2.5 percent) is associated with a 22-basis-point decline in monthly returns.

source.locator: section: Export Controls as Geoeconomic Shocks
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

payload.claim: Following export control events, a one standard deviation increase in exposure to affected U.S. suppliers is associated with a 31-basis-point decline in monthly returns for passive funds, compared with a 22-basis-point decline for active funds.
payload.quote: For a one standard deviation increase in exposure, passive funds experience a 31-basis-point decline in monthly returns, compared with 22 basis points for active funds.

source.locator: section: Mutual Funds Respond by Rebalancing Away from Geoeconomic Risk
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

payload.claim: In the month following an export control event, passive funds with exposure to affected U.S. suppliers experience outflows equivalent to about 0.35 percent of assets, while active funds experience statistically insignificant outflows.
payload.quote: In the following month, passive funds also experience outflows equivalent to about 0.35 percent of assets, while the outflows from active funds are statistically insignificant.

source.locator: section: Mutual Funds Respond by Rebalancing Away from Geoeconomic Risk
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

payload.claim: A long-short equity portfolio that buys U.S. firms with prior exposure to export controls and shorts unexposed firms earns about 1 percent per month in abnormal returns after adjusting for standard risk factors.
payload.quote: A long-short portfolio that buys firms previously exposed to export controls and shorts unexposed firms earns about 1 percent per month in abnormal returns after adjusting for standard risk factors.

source.locator: section: Is Geoeconomic Risk Priced In?
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

payload.claim: On average, U.S. domestic equity mutual funds invest 20.3 percent of their assets in U.S. firms that have at least one Chinese customer.
payload.quote: On average, 20.3 percent of fund assets are invested in U.S. firms with at least one Chinese customer.

source.locator: section: Geoeconomic Risk in Domestic Portfolios
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

testability.notes: Descriptive statistic rather than a directional trading rule, but directly testable with the named data.

payload.claim: Science and technology mutual funds invest 43.3 percent of their portfolios in domestic firms connected to Chinese customers.
payload.quote: For example, science and technology funds invest 43.3 percent of their portfolios in domestic firms that are connected to Chinese customers.

source.locator: section: Geoeconomic Risk in Domestic Portfolios
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

payload.claim: Within China-connected mutual fund portfolios, U.S. suppliers to Chinese customers newly targeted by export controls account for 8.4 percent of assets.
payload.quote: Within these China-connected portfolios, U.S. suppliers to Chinese customers newly targeted by export controls account for 8.4 percent of assets.

source.locator: section: Geoeconomic Risk in Domestic Portfolios
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

payload.claim: Active mutual fund managers continue selling affected U.S. suppliers for at least three months after an export control announcement rather than treating the price decline as a purely temporary idiosyncratic shock.
payload.quote: The selling of affected U.S. suppliers, still visible three months after the export controls, suggests that managers do not generally treat the price decline as a purely temporary idiosyncratic shock.

source.locator: section: Mutual Funds Respond by Rebalancing Away from Geoeconomic Risk
source.title: Navigating Geoeconomic Risk in the U.S. Stock Market

data_required: CRSP Mutual Fund Database holdings over multiple months

payload.claim: Following export control shocks, specialist mutual fund managers and higher-fee funds experience smaller performance declines, while traditional market-timing and stock-picking skill measures do not predict better outcomes.
payload.quote: Specialist managers and higher-fee funds experience smaller performance declines after export control shocks, while traditional market-timing and stock-picking skills do not predict better outcomes.

correction-2026-10-02-retrial-path: The correction-2026-09-30-pbo-family-kill note, registry entry 68485 (2026-10-01T11:31:24Z), names the existing D9 re-trial path for re-trying the five strategies it describes. For these five, that path cannot re-register the buried compositions themselves. This note records why, and the form their re-trial takes instead. It changes no verdict, no state, no invariant and no gate.

WHAT THE CORRECTION NOTE COMMITTED TO. It states: "Each of the five is instead re-tried as a NEW strategy id through the existing D9 re-trial path, once the standalone gauntlet worker is live." Under the D9 rule of family-openness-v1, registry entry 16071, a buried composition matched by its composition fingerprint registers again as a new strategy, either past a six-month data window or at the unified re-run of the whole registry that D8 pre-declares.

WHY THE BURIED COMPOSITIONS CANNOT BE REGISTERED AGAIN. All five buried registrations are version 1 and carry an exit/time_stop block with max_bars 20: b09adeb0be6faf4e at chain line 4957, 9acf68e5a2ef607d at 4973, 7ecf180b7e8b05ce at 4989, 6aebc4b7f051baba at 5005 and 15595642e7a2caaa at 23187. The exit-rules-v7 note, chain line 32897 (2026-09-04T01:31:27Z), retires exit/time_stop and arms a verifier rule: from the first registration after it, every strategy_registered must carry version 2 and no retired block type. verify_registry.py invariant 10 enforces that rule. Registering a buried composition again means a version-1 entry carrying exit/time_stop after line 32897, and invariant 10 rejects it on both counts. Raising only the version still leaves the retired exit, and exit-rules-v7 states that the composition fingerprint carries the version, so that entry would not be the buried composition either. The chain is append-only, so an entry that invariant 10 rejects would leave it INVALID for good. The buried compositions cannot be chained again.

WHAT HAPPENS INSTEAD. The five are re-tried in the unified re-run that D8 pre-declares and D9 governs, in the form exit-rules-v7 gives every composition carrying a retired exit. In the words of that chained note's disposition (D15(b)), everything "is re-trialled under the new grammar inside the unified re-run that D8 pre-declares and D9 governs", and a legacy composition that is not compliant as it stands "is to be proposed again through the Composer with a declared exit set, as a version-2 specification, and enters the queue as a D9 re-trial: a NEW strategy id and a new number, carrying none of the old record." The five carry exit/time_stop, so none of them is compliant as it stands. Each is re-tried as a version-2 composition with an exit set that exit-rules-v7 permits: a D9 re-trial in the form exit-rules-v7 gives it, not a second registration of the buried composition. Firing the re-trial is Coen-gated, as exit-rules-v7 states.

WHAT STILL HOLDS FROM THE CORRECTION NOTE. Each re-tried composition is a NEW strategy id, charged to N in full. It goes through the screen and, if it passes, is judged by all six gates from scratch on the data then current. It inherits nothing from the buried entry, neither its verdict nor its passing of the gates. The five graveyard entries stand, and nothing is moved out of the graveyard. Because its exit differs, a re-tried composition is not the buried one, and its result says nothing about the buried composition's exit.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE. No verdict, no lifecycle state, no invariant and no gate. It loosens nothing: invariant 10 stays exactly as chained, and the five are re-tried under it, not exempted from it. Every other statement of the correction note stands.

WHEN. The commitment in entry 68485 to re-try the five is discharged when the unified re-run registers their version-2 compositions. That replaces the condition "once the standalone gauntlet worker is live" in entry 68485. This note sets no date.

payload.claim: Companies that allow CEOs personal use of the corporate jet experience stock price underperformance of about 4% per year relative to firms that do not.
payload.quote: And what a study found was that companies where they allowed a personal usage of the jet, the stock price fell by about 4% per year, applied to the average value of $7.5 billion. That is $300 million of underperformance.

source.title: The Hidden Warning Sign in a CEO’s Private Jet

data_required: SEC disclosures of personal aircraft use (proxy statements)
historical stock price returns for affected companies
matched sample of companies without personal jet usage disclosure
testability.notes: Study referenced but not named; underlying source and sample period not specified in the quote.

payload.claim: The relative size of a CEO's photo in the annual report compared to other top management team members, and whether a CEO uses 'I' rather than 'we' in communications, are data-reinforced measures of CEO power that could be associated with company outcomes.
payload.quote: And the Chapter 7 goes and looks at many other seemingly trivial, but actually data-reinforced measures of CEO power, which could be the size of your photo in the annual report compared to the rest of your top management team. Because that might suggest, I don’t need to listen to my colleagues, whether the CEO refers to I rather than we.

source.title: The Hidden Warning Sign in a CEO’s Private Jet

data_required: CEO language/text from shareholder letters or calls
testability.notes: Measures are described as part of a referenced book chapter without specifying the underlying study's methodology or results in the quote.

payload.text:
gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-1: Amends gauntlet-protocol-v6.1, chained at registry entry 68486, in two things the gauntlet_stats entries record: the expected maximum Sharpe ratio behind the recorded deflated Sharpe is floored, and the PBO permutation null is built by a stated rule for every family that has a verdict needing statistics. It also records that the clustering was made faster without changing any result. Everything else in v6.1, and in v6 as v6.1 left it, stands as written. No gate is added, removed or re-tuned, no threshold moves, and no verdict or state change is touched. Pre-declared before the first gauntlet_stats entry exists: pipeline/gauntlet_stats.py refuses to chain any gauntlet_stats entry until this note is on the chain.

WHAT v6.1 SAYS. Its paragraph HOW trials_n IS RECORDED floors the effective trials count trials_n at the highest cluster count already on the chain, records the clustering's own argmax as trials_n_raw, and says of the cross-cluster Sharpe variance: "trials_sr_var is computed from the current clustering and is not floored". The deflated Sharpe on a gauntlet_stats entry is psr(sr_hat, SR*, T, skew, kurt), where SR* = expected_max_sharpe(trials_n, trials_sr_var) is the expected maximum Sharpe of trials_n zero-skill trials. In pipeline/stats.py, SR* is the square root of trials_sr_var times a factor that depends on trials_n alone, so SR* is proportional to the square root of trials_sr_var.

THE MEASURED PROBLEM. The silhouette quality curve that picks k has two peaks of nearly equal height at very different k: a coarse one below about 100 clusters and a fine one at a few hundred. Which one wins depends on the registry, and trials_sr_var moves with it. On a copy of the registry and the simulation cache, on a random sample of 4,000 registered strategies, the argmax was k = 398 with quality 1.73831 while k = 23 scored 1.73289, 0.31 percent lower. On registration-order prefixes of the same copy, clustered with the full registry's common window held fixed, the argmax moved between the two peaks as strategies were added, and trials_sr_var moved by about three orders of magnitude: 6.5e-4 at 2,000 strategies (k = 162) and 5.8e-7 at 5,000 strategies (k = 6). On the same copy at data vintage 2026-09-27, over all 13,730 registered strategies, the argmax is the fine peak, k = 560 with quality 1.81564 and trials_sr_var 4.64e-4; the coarse peak is k = 82 with quality 1.70483, 6.1 percent lower, and its clusters give trials_sr_var 1.17e-6, about 395 times smaller. The chain records the same movement. The 1,003 gauntlet-protocol-v6 verdicts that recorded trials_n 302 (registered_n 6,075) recorded trials_sr_var 5.55e-4 and SR* 0.0683; the 676 that recorded trials_n 44 (registered_n 11,860) recorded trials_sr_var 2.04e-6 and SR* 0.00318, about 21 times smaller. trials_n is now floored and trials_sr_var is not, so a night whose argmax lands on the coarse peak would pair the floored N with a coarse-peak variance, and SR* would fall by the square root of the variance ratio: about 30 times for a ratio of 1,000, and about 20 times (0.0665 to 0.00334 at N = 560) for the ratio measured on the full registry. A smaller SR* makes the recorded deflated Sharpe more lenient. Left as it is, the recorded deflated Sharpe could become more lenient as the registry grows, which is what the trials_n floor was introduced to prevent.

THE CHANGE TO SR*. From this note onward the SR* used for the recorded deflated Sharpe on a gauntlet_stats entry is expected_max_sharpe, the larger of expected_max_sharpe_raw and expected_max_sharpe_floor. expected_max_sharpe_raw is expected_max_sharpe(trials_n, trials_sr_var) computed exactly as v6.1 computes it: trials_n floored as v6.1 says, trials_sr_var from the current clustering. expected_max_sharpe_floor is the highest SR* already on this chain: expected_max_sharpe on gauntlet verdicts under protocols v3, v4, v5 and v6, the protocols whose trials_n sets the trials_n floor, and expected_max_sharpe_raw on earlier gauntlet_stats entries. A value that is not a number, is a boolean, is not finite or is not above zero is never a floor. The entry that supplied the floor is named by expected_max_sharpe_floor_entry_hash; on a tie it is the first. Every gauntlet_stats entry records expected_max_sharpe_raw, expected_max_sharpe_floor, expected_max_sharpe_floor_entry_hash and expected_max_sharpe, and keeps trials_n, trials_n_raw, trials_n_floor, trials_n_floor_entry_hash and trials_sr_var exactly as v6.1 records them. trials_sr_var itself is still not floored: the floor acts on SR*, the only quantity through which trials_sr_var reaches the deflated Sharpe. The Harvey-Liu haircut reads trials_n and not SR*, and is unchanged. From this note onward the SR* behind the recorded deflated Sharpe never falls from one gauntlet_stats entry to a later one. At the time of this note, read from a copy of the chain, the highest SR* on the chain is 0.06883413189134865, recorded by 650 gauntlet-protocol-v6 verdicts, the first of them at registry entry 9829 (2026-08-25T23:23:48Z, trials_n 154, registered_n 1,815). The clustering of the 2026-10-03 run, reproduced on a copy at data vintage 2026-09-27 over 13,730 registered strategies, gives trials_n_raw 560 and expected_max_sharpe_raw 0.0665, below that floor.

THE PBO NULL IS BUILT FOR EVERY FAMILY THAT NEEDS STATISTICS. The v6.1 implementation recorded PBO with the gauntlet's helpers and arguments and, as the gauntlet did, built the permutation null only for a family with a passing verdict among the verdicts being statted in that run. A family with no passing verdict in that run recorded pbo_status not_measured_dead_group, whether or not it was measurable, so siblings statted on different nights could record different pbo_status for the same family. From this note onward, for every family that holds at least one v6.1 verdict without a gauntlet_stats entry, the permutation null is built whenever the family is measurable, that is, whenever its observed PBO exists and it has at least four distinct configurations, whether or not any of its verdicts passed. A measurable family records pbo_status measured, or underpowered if its null yields no value. A family that is not measurable records pbo_status underpowered. pbo_status not_measured_dead_group, which the previous rule recorded for a family with no passing verdict in the run, is no longer recorded. The PBO fields then depend only on the family's members and their train-window series, with the null seeded by the family id as before, so siblings statted on different nights record the same values while the family and its data are unchanged. Each family's result is kept for the current data vintage and data digest, keyed also on a hash of the family's inputs and one of the PBO code and constants, and reused. Its null is therefore built once per vintage only while the family's membership, its data and that code are unchanged; a family that gains a member within a vintage gets a new null. The measurement that decided the rule, on a copy of the chain at data vintage 2026-09-27: the 2,193 v6.1 verdicts then without statistics belonged to 286 families, all 286 measurable and 31 of them with a passing verdict. Timed on six of those families, a null cost about 56 times the family's observed PBO computation, which projects to about 32,300 seconds for all 286 families against about 5,000 seconds for the 31. The job has 5.75 hours a night and resumes the next night, so that backlog is projected to clear in about two nights.

THE CLUSTERING IS UNCHANGED, ONLY FASTER. The bookkeeping inside the agglomeration in pipeline/cluster.py now keeps each cluster's best merge candidate in arrays and resolves ties with arrays, and the distance arithmetic runs in place. The distance, the average linkage, the tie-break on the distance rounded to 12 decimals and then on the pair of the two clusters' smallest strategy ids, the range of k from 2 to n minus 1, the silhouette quality score and the set of clustered strategies, every buried one included, are untouched. tools/verify_cluster_identity.py showed the change bit-identical on real data. It was run on a copy of the chain with the simulation cache read only, at data vintage 2026-09-27, on random samples of 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000 of the 13,730 registered strategies, and for each the full merge history, k, the cluster labels, trials_sr_var and expected_max_sharpe(k, trials_sr_var) were identical to the previous code bit for bit. The full registry was run with the new code only, not compared against the previous code: on the same copy the clustering of all 13,730 strategies (cluster.effective_trials) took 118 seconds and returned k = 560, the argmax the 2026-10-03 run logged; that run's clustering stage had taken 14,927 seconds.

RATCHET POSITION. No gate reads trials_n, SR*, the deflated Sharpe, PBO, plateau_ok or the haircut, under v6.1 or here, so nothing a gate decides changes and nothing loosens. The SR* floor can only raise SR*, so it can only lower the recorded deflated Sharpe: it is stricter, never more lenient. Building the null for more families records more and decides nothing. pipeline/gauntlet_stats.py refuses to chain (exit 1, exit_reason refused_no_amendment_note) until this note is on the chain, detected by the prefix gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-1: of its first line, first occurrence. The gauntlet worker's refusal check, the rollback gauntlet's family-kill switch and verify_registry.py invariant 12 detect the v6.1 addendum by the prefix gauntlet-protocol-v6.1: with the colon straight after v6.1; this note has a hyphen in that place, so it arms none of them. Runs without --chain are unaffected.

payload.claim: Increases in implied Treasury volatility (measured by the MOVE Index) predict lower Treasury returns over the next trading day, while decreases in implied volatility predict higher next-day Treasury returns.
payload.quote: Their main finding: Increases in implied bond volatility predict lower subsequent Treasury returns, while decreases predict higher returns. Importantly, this is a short-horizon effect: The paper focuses on whether changes in implied volatility contain information about Treasury returns over the next trading day.

source.locator: intro section, discussing Kodithyala and Rebonato (2026) paper
source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

testability.notes: This is the paper's finding being reported/endorsed by the author.

payload.claim: Large changes in implied Treasury volatility (MOVE Index) show the strongest estimated relationship with subsequent Treasury returns compared to smaller changes.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

payload.claim: The negative predictive relationship between changes in implied Treasury volatility and subsequent Treasury returns holds across Treasury maturities, though its strength varies along the yield curve.
payload.quote: The predictive relationship is negative across Treasury maturities, although its strength varies along the yield curve.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

payload.claim: A strategy dynamically adjusting Treasury exposure based on changes in the MOVE Index, tested over Treasury and MOVE data from April 1988 through May 2026, produces higher Sharpe ratios than unconditional (static) Treasury exposure.
payload.quote: The paper uses Treasury and MOVE data from April 1988 through May 2026 and finds that a strategy dynamically adjusting Treasury exposure based on changes in MOVE produces higher Sharpe ratios than unconditional Treasury exposure.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

payload.claim: In a 60% SPY / 40% TLT portfolio rebalanced monthly, rotating the TLT allocation into cash when the standardized daily change in VXTLT (z-score) exceeds a threshold of 1, 1.5, or 2 standard deviations constitutes a testable overlay strategy.
payload.quote:
I apply the signal to a traditional portfolio invested
60% in SPY and 40% in TLT
, rebalanced monthly. Normally, the bond allocation remains invested in TLT.
Instead, I rotate from TLT into cash when the VXTLT signal exceeds the threshold:
\( z_t > c, \qquad c \in \{1,\;1.5,\;2\}. \)

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

payload.claim: Using the official daily VXTLT close signal (close-to-close execution) with a 1-standard-deviation threshold on a 60/40 SPY/TLT portfolio over December 2013 to September 2026 increases CAGR from 8.99% to 10.40%, raises the Sharpe ratio from 0.68 to 0.80, and improves maximum drawdown from about -27% to -25%.
payload.quote: At the 1-standard-deviation threshold, CAGR increases from 8.99% to 10.40%, while the Sharpe ratio rises from 0.68 to 0.80. Maximum drawdown also improves somewhat from about−27% to −25%.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

testability.notes: Sample period December 2013 to September 2026 per surrounding text.

payload.claim: Using the open-to-close execution version of the VXTLT signal (observing the official close and trading at the next day's open) with a 2-standard-deviation threshold on the 60/40 SPY/TLT portfolio achieves a CAGR of 10.55% and a Sharpe ratio of 0.82, compared to 0.68 for the standard 60/40 portfolio.
payload.quote: Interestingly, the effect survives this delay. At the 2-standard-deviation threshold, CAGR reaches 10.55%, and the Sharpe ratio rises to 0.82, compared to a Sharpe of 0.68 for the standard 60/40 portfolio.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

payload.claim: Using the 15:45 ET pre-close VXTLT signal (close-to-close execution, implementable via market-on-close orders) with a 1-standard-deviation threshold on the 60/40 SPY/TLT portfolio over the post-May-2020 sample increases CAGR from 6.84% to 8.54%, improves the Sharpe ratio from 0.36 to 0.50, and improves maximum drawdown from -27% to -25%.
payload.quote: At the 1-standard-deviation threshold, CAGR increases from 6.84% to 8.54%, the Sharpe ratio improves from 0.36 to 0.50, and maximum drawdown again improves somewhat from −27% to −25%.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

testability.notes: Shorter sample from May 2020 due to 5-minute VXTLT data availability.

payload.claim: Across three execution assumptions (daily close close-to-close, daily close open-to-close, and 15:45 close-to-close) and three signal thresholds (1, 1.5, 2 standard deviations), all nine net-of-cost VXTLT-based overlay variants improve CAGR, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown relative to the standard 60/40 SPY/TLT baseline, after accounting for transaction costs.
payload.quote: Across the three execution assumptions and three signal thresholds, all nine net-of-cost overlays improve CAGR, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown relative to their corresponding 60/40 baseline.

source.title: Can Bond Volatility Improve a 60/40 Portfolio?

payload.claim: The largest performance improvements from the VXTLT-based overlay on the 60/40 portfolio occur during stressed bond-market periods, notably 2020 and 2022.

payload.claim: A strategy that buys a stock at the next market open on Tuesday when, at Monday's close, the stock closed more than 1% below its opening price and the closing price was above the previous bar's 200-day simple moving average, is a testable mean-reversion entry rule for individual stocks.
payload.quote:
The day of the week is Monday
The stock closes more than 1% below its opening price:
Close[0] < 0.99 × Open[0]
The closing price is above the previous bar’s 200-day simple moving average:
Close[0] > SMA(200)[1]
All three conditions must be true. The position opens at the next market open, on Tuesday, using a Market order.

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily OHLC price data for individual stocks

payload.claim: A position exit rule where the position is closed when today's closing price exceeds the closing price from two bars ago, or when a 10 daily bar holding limit is reached (with no stop loss or profit target), is a testable rule for closing mean-reversion stock trades.
payload.quote:
The position closes when either condition occurs first:
Today’s closing price is higher than the closing price two bars ago:
Close[0] > Close[2]
The position reaches the holding limit of 10 daily bars
Stop Loss and Profit Target are disabled.

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily OHLC price data for individual stocks

payload.claim: Ranking qualifying stocks by a Position score equal to one minus the five-period Rate of Change (prioritizing stocks with the weakest recent five-period performance) is a testable method for selecting among candidates when more stocks qualify than available position slots.
payload.quote: The formula is one minus the five-period ROC, or Rate of Change. A lower ROC produces a higher score, giving priority to qualifying stocks with the weakest recent performance.

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily close prices for individual stocks

payload.claim: Backtesting the Tuesday Reversal strategy on a basket of Nasdaq 100 stocks over 20 years of daily data with 0.1% commission, starting from $10,000, produced approximately $55,000 net profit, about 5,900 trades, nearly 10% CAGR, a profit factor of 1.35, and a 66% win rate.
payload.quote:
The first test used a basket of Nasdaq 100 stocks, daily data, 20 years of history, and a commission of 0.1%.
Starting with $10,000, the backtest reported:
Net profit: approximately $55,000
Trades: approximately 5,900
CAGR: almost 10%
Profit factor: 1.35
Win rate: 66%

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily price data for Nasdaq 100 constituent stocks (20-year history)

payload.claim: In the Nasdaq 100 backtest of the Tuesday Reversal strategy, the average winning trade made $54 and the average losing trade lost $79, reflecting a profile where losses exceed wins despite a high win rate.
payload.quote: The average winning trade made $54, while the average losing trade lost $79. The strategy won frequently, but its losses were larger than its wins—a typical mean reversion profile.

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily price data for Nasdaq 100 constituent stocks

payload.claim: In the Nasdaq 100 backtest of the Tuesday Reversal strategy, average holding time was under three days overall, with winning trades lasting about two days and losing trades lasting almost five days.
payload.quote: Average holding time was under three days, despite the 10-bar limit. Winners lasted about two days, while losers lasted almost five. Successful rebounds produced quick exits; unsuccessful trades stayed open longer and could reach the time limit.

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily price data for Nasdaq 100 constituent stocks

payload.claim: When SPY is scaled to match the Tuesday Reversal strategy's historical dollar drawdown on Nasdaq 100 stocks, the strategy achieves a Sharpe ratio of 1.02 versus 0.65 for SPY, a CAGR/maximum drawdown ratio of 0.76 versus 0.24, and approximately 66% market exposure versus 100% for SPY.
payload.quote:
Sharpe ratio: 1.02 for the strategy versus 0.65 for SPY
CAGR / maximum drawdown: 0.76 versus 0.24
Exposure: approximately 66% versus 100%

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily price data for Nasdaq 100 constituent stocks

payload.claim: When SPY is scaled to match the Tuesday Reversal strategy's percentage drawdown, the strategy's net profit of approximately $55,000 compares to approximately $11,500 for SPY over the same period.
payload.quote: The report also showed a separate comparison with SPY scaled to match the strategy’s percentage drawdown. In that comparison, net profit was approximately $55,000 versus $11,500.

source.title: Tuesday Reversal Strategy: Tested on Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 Stocks

data_required: daily price data for Nasdaq 100 constituent stocks

payload.claim: Applying the identical Tuesday Reversal strategy rules (entry conditions, exits, Position score, max positions, test period) to a basket of S&P 500 stocks instead of Nasdaq 100 produced approximately 8,000 trades and a CAGR of 15%, about five percentage points higher than the Nasdaq 100 result.
payload.quote:
Next, we changed the stock basket to the S&P 500. Everything else stayed the same: entry conditions, exits, Position score, maximum positions, and test period.
The result was approximately 8,000 trades and a CAGR of 15%—about five percentage points higher than on Nasdaq 100.

payload.claim: BORR's combination of a sharp EBITDA break, negative free cash flow, 6.1x net debt/EBITDA leverage, 3.6x EV/revenue, and -4.7% FCF yield (despite 98.7% technical utilization in 2025) supported a sell rating as of the September 2026 publication date.
payload.quote: I rated BORR a sell because the latest quarter showed a sharp EBITDA break and negative free cash flow, even though the fleet-quality case was still supported by 98.7% technical utilization in 2025. My concern was that 6.1x net debt/EBITDA left too little room if dayrates softened again, and I also thought the valuation looked stretched at 3.6x EV/revenue with a -4.7% FCF yield.

source.title: The Scorecard: 1 Month Update: BORR Sell — Correct so far

payload.claim: A sustained recovery in BORR's operating numbers, specifically quarterly EBITDA back above $100M and free cash flow positive for two consecutive quarters, would materially weaken the sell case on BORR.
payload.quote: If BORR can show a sustained recovery in the operating numbers I highlighted — especially quarterly EBITDA back above $100M and free cash flow positive for two straight quarters — my sell case would weaken materially.

source.locator: What Could Still Prove Me Wrong
source.title: The Scorecard: 1 Month Update: BORR Sell — Correct so far

payload.claim: BORR quarterly revenue stabilizing above roughly $250M combined with easing balance-sheet pressure would suggest the company's recent operating break was temporary rather than structural, weakening the sell thesis.
payload.quote: I would also be less confident if revenue stabilizes above roughly $250M per quarter and the balance-sheet pressure starts to ease, because that would suggest the recent break was temporary rather than structural.

source.locator: What Could Still Prove Me Wrong

payload.claim: An equal-weight short position on D+1 (day after U.S. federal elections) across a seven-asset ETF basket yields 1.86% per annum with a Sharpe of 0.31 and a maximum drawdown of -4.16%, achieved over 13 trading days spanning 26 years.
payload.quote: An equal-weight short on D+1 yields 1.86% per annum with a Sharpe of 0.31 and a maximum drawdown of -4.16%, achieved over 13 trading days in 26 years.

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

payload.claim: An equal-weight long position held on Election Day (D0) across the diversified ETF basket earns 1.03% per annum at a Sharpe of 0.19.
payload.quote: an equal-weight D0 long earns a modest 1.03% p.a. at a Sharpe of 0.19, which we document as the control arm of the experiment but do not trade

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

payload.claim: Intermediate Treasuries (IEF) sell off in the four days before U.S. federal elections and rally from Election Day through two days after, producing a Sharpe ratio of 0.48.
payload.quote: Intermediate Treasuries exhibit the inverse pattern, selling off in the four days before the vote and rallying from D0 to D+2, with a Sharpe of 0.48.

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

payload.claim: Across U.S. presidential election cycles from 1992 to 2008, the VIX rose with the probability of the eventual winner.
payload.quote:
Goodell and Vähämaa (2013)
establish the build-up: across U.S. presidential cycles from 1992 to 2008, VIX rose with the probability of the eventual winner — political anxiety bought in advance, priced in volatility points rather than votes.

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

testability.notes: Cited from Goodell and Vähämaa (2013), endorsed as foundational premise.

payload.claim: U.S. equity premiums in post-midterm-election months average 15.41% annualized versus 2.98% annualized in other months, with Treasury premiums lower as political uncertainty clears.
payload.quote:
Chan and Marsh (2021
) widen the tape: U.S. midterm elections command at least the same asset-pricing premium, with equity premiums averaging 15.41% annualized in post-midterm months against 2.98% elsewhere, and Treasury premiums lower as uncertainty clears.

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

testability.notes: Cited from Chan and Marsh (2021).

payload.claim: U.S. equities drift up approximately 2.5% in the six trading days leading into Election Day, a pattern that compounded a $10,000 investment to $22,500 over 210 total event-days from 1950 to 2018.
payload.quote:
Vojtko and Cisár (2020)
show U.S. equities drift up about 2.5% in the six days into Election Day, turning $10k into $22.5k over 210 days from 1950-2018.

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

data_required: U.S. equity index daily price data 1950-2018
testability.notes: Cited from the authors' own prior study (Vojtko and Cisár, 2020).

payload.claim: Individual D+1 short positions across the multi-asset election basket range from +0.13% (tech, XLK-SPY) to +1.81% (emerging markets, EEM-SPY) per trade, each contributing positively to the equal-weight basket's 1.86% p.a. performance across nine full-coverage election cycles (2008-2024).
payload.quote: No leg freeloads: per-trade D+1 shorts run from +0.13% in tech to +1.81% in EM. The basket isn’t carried; it’s broad; the equal-weight basket compounds to 1.86% p.a., 0.31 Sharpe and only –4.16% max DD across nine full-coverage cycles.

source.title: Trading the Multi-Asset Drift Around U.S. Elections

payload.claim: A one-session long position on Election Day (D0) in the same seven-asset basket produces 1.03% p.a. with Sharpe 0.19 and max drawdown -5.83%, with crisis hedges (GLD, USO, UDN) carrying all the drift while equity spreads remain near zero, and the statistical significance is thin (t \u2248 1.1) with November 2008 driving most cumulative equity.
payload.quote: Flipping the trade — long the same basket on D0 for one session — prints 1.03% p.a., Sharpe 0.19, MaxDD −5.83%: crisis hedges (GLD, USO, UDN) carry all the drift, equity spreads hover at zero, and November 2008 delivers most of the curve’s equity in a single day (Figure 3, Table 1). Real but thin, t ≈ 1.1.

payload.claim: A reversal strategy can be defined using the difference between two exponential moving averages normalized by ATR to identify a market regime, combined with a condition of negative momentum over the previous five days.

This makes the signal comparable across stocks with different prices and volatility levels. A second condition looks for negative momentum over the previous five days.
